name: Atypical Spitz tumour
aliases: Spitz tumour of uncertain malignant potential
Spitzoid tumour of uncertain malignant potential

clinicalPearls: A melanocytic tumour of intermediate (uncertain) malignant potential, sitting biologically between a benign Spitz naevus and spitzoid melanoma
Composed of large epithelioid and/or spindled melanocytes with abundant cytoplasm, but showing some atypical features that fall short of unequivocal melanoma
Most often affects children, adolescents and young adults, commonly on the extremities, though it can occur at any age
Genetically defined by kinase fusions involving ALK, ROS1, NTRK1, NTRK3, BRAF, MET or RET, or by HRAS mutation, typically in the absence of the mutations seen in conventional melanoma
Ancillary tests such as fluorescence in situ hybridisation and comparative genomic hybridisation help stratify risk but cannot always definitively separate benign from malignant lesions
Sentinel lymph node biopsy may show nodal deposits, yet this does not carry the same grave prognosis as in conventional melanoma
Complete excision with clear margins is the mainstay of management given the diagnostic uncertainty
reference.pathophysiology: Atypical Spitz tumours arise from melanocytes and are characterised by activating kinase fusions or, less often, HRAS mutation, which drive the distinctive large spitzoid cell morphology. These alterations differ from the classic driver mutations of conventional melanoma, and the tumours occupy an intermediate position in which some show additional chromosomal changes (such as certain copy-number gains or losses) that shift them towards malignant behaviour. Because the morphological and molecular findings overlap with both benign Spitz naevi and spitzoid melanoma, no single feature reliably predicts outcome, and risk is assessed by combining histology with ancillary genetic studies.
additionalInvestigations: Complete excision biopsy allowing full architectural and cytological assessment
Immunohistochemistry including melanocytic markers and proliferation index, with p16 evaluation
Fluorescence in situ hybridisation for melanoma-associated copy-number changes
Array comparative genomic hybridisation to detect chromosomal aberrations aiding risk stratification
Molecular testing for kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK, BRAF, RET, MET) and HRAS status
Consideration of sentinel lymph node biopsy in selected higher-risk lesions, interpreted with caution
redFlags: Large size, ulceration, deep extension or a high mitotic rate suggesting spitzoid melanoma
Accumulation of multiple chromosomal aberrations on molecular testing
Marked cytological atypia with atypical mitotic figures
Rapid growth or change in a previously stable lesion
reference.prognosis: Most atypical Spitz tumours behave in an indolent fashion and, when completely excised, follow a favourable course; even with positive sentinel nodes the outcome is generally far better than for conventional melanoma, but a minority behave aggressively, so the intermediate category reflects genuine uncertainty and warrants complete excision and clinical follow-up.
pitfalls: Overcalling the lesion as melanoma and prompting unnecessarily aggressive treatment
Undercalling a true spitzoid melanoma as a benign or atypical Spitz tumour
Interpreting a positive sentinel lymph node as carrying the same prognosis as in conventional melanoma
Relying on morphology alone without ancillary molecular and cytogenetic studies in ambiguous cases
Leaving positive margins because the lesion was assumed to be entirely benign
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Skin Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Melanocytic Tumours
management: Complete surgical excision with adequate clear margins as the mainstay of treatment
Re-excision or wide local excision where margins are positive or inadequate
Ancillary molecular studies, fluorescence in situ hybridisation and comparative genomic hybridisation to stratify malignant potential and guide treatment intensity
Selective sentinel lymph node biopsy in higher-risk lesions, interpreted cautiously as nodal deposits do not carry the grave prognosis of conventional melanoma
Surveillance with periodic skin and regional nodal examination for local or nodal recurrence
In the rare lesion behaving as melanoma, targeted therapy against the driver kinase fusion (ALK, NTRK, ROS1) may be considered
Multidisciplinary dermatopathology and oncology review for atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions
